quests.question: She is one of those teachers who ___ students to think independently.
quests.hint: The verb in the relative clause agrees with 'teachers' (plural), not 'one'.
quests.explanation: In 'one of those [plural noun] who/that', the verb in the relative clause agrees with the plural noun. 'Those teachers' is plural, so 'who encourage' is correct.

quests.question: He is one of those managers who ___ every decision personally.
quests.hint: Wait - the verb agrees with 'managers' (plural) in 'one of those who' constructions.
quests.explanation: In 'one of those [plural noun] who', the relative clause verb agrees with the plural noun, not 'one'. 'Managers' is plural, so 'who make' is correct. Note: 'makes' would be wrong here.

quests.question: She is one of those athletes who ___ every day without fail.
quests.hint: Focus: does the relative clause verb agree with 'one' or with 'athletes'?
quests.explanation: In 'one of those athletes who train', the verb 'train' agrees with 'athletes' (plural), not with 'one' (singular). The relative clause modifies the plural noun.

quests.question: She is the only one of the students who ___ fluent in three languages.
quests.hint: With 'the only one of', the verb agrees with 'one' (singular), not the plural noun.
quests.explanation: 'The only one of' is different from 'one of those'. Here, only one person has the quality, so the verb in the relative clause agrees with 'one' - singular: 'the only one who is'.

quests.question: He is the only one of the applicants who ___ all the criteria.
quests.hint: 'The only one of' - the relative clause verb agrees with 'one', not 'applicants'.
quests.explanation: With 'the only one of [plural noun] who', the verb agrees with 'one', not the plural noun. 'One' is singular, so 'meets' is correct.

quests.question: Swimming in cold water ___ good for your immune system.
quests.hint: A gerund phrase ('Swimming...') acting as the subject is always singular.
quests.explanation: When a gerund or gerund phrase acts as the subject of a sentence, it is treated as singular. 'Swimming is good' - the gerund phrase takes a singular verb.

quests.question: Learning two languages at the same time ___ possible.
quests.hint: The gerund phrase 'Learning two languages at the same time' is the subject - singular.
quests.explanation: A gerund phrase as subject is always singular. 'Learning two languages is possible' - not 'are possible'.

quests.question: To understand grammar rules ___ essential for good writing.
quests.hint: An infinitive phrase ('To understand...') as the subject is always singular.
quests.explanation: An infinitive phrase acting as the subject is always singular. 'To understand grammar rules is essential' - not 'are essential'.

quests.question: Travelling by train ___ much cheaper than flying.
quests.hint: A gerund ('Travelling') as the subject takes a singular verb.
quests.explanation: A gerund acting as the subject is always singular. 'Travelling is much cheaper' - even though we can imagine many journeys.

quests.question: Cooking for large groups ___ very different from cooking at home.
quests.hint: The gerund phrase 'Cooking for large groups' is the subject - always singular.
quests.explanation: Gerund phrases as subjects always take singular verbs. 'Cooking for large groups is very different' - not 'are different'.

quests.question: Exercising regularly and eating well ___ key to staying healthy.
quests.hint: Two gerund phrases joined by 'and' form a plural compound subject.
quests.explanation: Two gerund phrases joined by 'and' create a plural compound subject. 'Exercising and eating are key' - just like two noun subjects joined by 'and'.

quests.question: It ___ important to read the contract before signing.
quests.hint: 'It' as a subject is always singular - even in 'it is important to...' constructions.
quests.explanation: When 'it' is used as a preparatory subject ('it is important to...'), the verb is always singular. This 'it' is a grammatical placeholder and is always singular.

quests.question: It ___ the scientists who made the breakthrough.
quests.hint: In a cleft sentence ('it was/were... who'), the verb after 'it' is usually singular.
quests.explanation: In a cleft sentence starting with 'it was/were', 'it' takes a singular verb. 'It was the scientists who made the breakthrough' is the standard form.

quests.question: It ___ clear that new measures were urgently needed.
quests.hint: 'It' as a subject is always singular - even in complex sentences.
quests.explanation: When 'it' introduces a sentence followed by an adjective and a clause, it is always singular. 'It was clear that...' is correct.

quests.question: Running a business and raising children ___ both very demanding.
quests.hint: Two separate activities joined by 'and' together make a plural subject.
quests.explanation: When two gerund phrases are joined by 'and', they form a plural compound subject - just like two nouns joined by 'and'. 'Running a business and raising children are both demanding'.

quests.question: The committee that ___ selected the candidates meets on Friday.
quests.hint: Inside the relative clause, 'that' refers to 'the committee' (singular collective).
quests.explanation: The relative clause 'that has selected the candidates' contains 'that', which refers to 'the committee' - a singular collective. The verb inside the clause is 'has'.

quests.question: The data that ___ collected over ten years is now available.
quests.hint: 'Data' treated as singular here - the relative clause verb agrees with it.
quests.explanation: When 'data' is treated as singular (common in modern usage), the relative clause verb is also singular: 'that was collected'. The verb in the relative clause agrees with its antecedent.

quests.question: The report that ___ presented yesterday raised many questions.
quests.hint: Inside the relative clause, 'that' refers to 'the report' (singular).
quests.explanation: 'That' in the relative clause refers to 'the report', which is singular. 'That was presented yesterday' - singular verb inside the clause.

quests.question: There ___ a series of issues to address before we can proceed.
quests.hint: The real subject after 'there' is 'a series of issues' - 'series' here is plural in meaning.
quests.explanation: Although 'series' can be singular, 'a series of issues' here refers to multiple issues, and in informal English 'there are a series of issues' is widely accepted.

quests.question: There ___ evidence that the treatment works.
quests.hint: 'Evidence' is uncountable - singular verb after 'there'.
quests.explanation: 'Evidence' is an uncountable noun. 'There is evidence' - uncountable nouns always take singular verbs.

quests.question: There ___ a number of ways to approach this problem.
quests.hint: 'A number of ways' means 'several ways' - plural verb.
quests.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several', so it takes a plural verb. 'There are a number of ways' - not 'there is'.

quests.question: The class that performs best ___ the prize.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the class' (singular) - the relative clause is descriptive.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'the class', a singular collective. The relative clause 'that performs best' describes which class but does not change the main verb agreement. 'The class wins'.

quests.question: The classes that perform best ___ the prizes.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the classes' (plural) - the relative clause is descriptive.
quests.explanation: 'The classes' is plural. The relative clause 'that perform best' describes them. Since 'classes' is plural, the main verb is 'win'.

quests.question: Being honest with people ___ always the right approach.
quests.hint: The gerund phrase 'Being honest with people' is the subject - singular.
quests.explanation: A gerund phrase as subject is always singular. 'Being honest is always the right approach' - not 'are'.

quests.question: None of the information ___ verified before publication.
quests.hint: In formal writing, 'none' with an uncountable noun ('information') takes a singular verb.
quests.explanation: In formal English, 'none of' with an uncountable noun takes a singular verb. 'None of the information was verified' - 'information' is uncountable.

quests.question: None of the witnesses ___ able to identify the suspect.
quests.hint: In modern English, 'none of the [plural noun]' commonly takes a plural verb.
quests.explanation: 'None of the witnesses' commonly takes a plural verb in modern English. 'None of the witnesses were able to identify' - this is widely accepted today.

quests.question: Any of the options ___ acceptable to the committee.
quests.hint: 'Any' with a singular meaning takes a singular verb.
quests.explanation: When 'any' means 'any single one', it takes a singular verb. 'Any of the options is acceptable' - meaning each option on its own would be fine.

quests.question: Any of the candidates ___ likely to succeed in this role.
quests.hint: When 'any' means 'all/every one', it takes a plural verb.
quests.explanation: When 'any' refers to all items in a group (meaning 'whichever you choose'), it can take a plural verb. 'Any of the candidates are likely to succeed' - all of them could.

quests.question: The problem that concerns me most ___ the lack of funding.
quests.hint: The subject is 'the problem' (singular) - the relative clause is descriptive.
quests.explanation: The subject is 'the problem'. The relative clause 'that concerns me most' describes which problem. 'The problem is the lack of funding' - singular subject, singular verb.

quests.question: Deciding which applicant to hire ___ never easy.
quests.hint: The gerund phrase 'Deciding which applicant to hire' acts as a singular subject.
quests.explanation: A gerund phrase as subject is always singular. 'Deciding which applicant to hire is never easy' - not 'are never easy'.
